title: TCP U2·W1 — Property Transactions & Basis Planning (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — controlling gain, character, and basis

Property transactions are where a planner's leverage is greatest: by choosing when to recognize gain, managing its character, and engineering basis, large tax can be deferred or eliminated entirely. REG stated the property rules; TCP turns them into strategy. For MBG's owner Jordan Reed — holding appreciating land, equipment, and a residence — the deferral and step-up techniques here are worth more than most income-side moves. All figures use the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline.

Basis fundamentals as a planning variable

Basis is the number subtracted from the amount realized to compute gain, so managing it is managing tax. Cost basis is adjusted up for improvements and down for depreciation. Gifted property takes a carryover basis (with the dual-basis rule for losses), preserving built-in gain; inherited property takes a §1014 stepped-up basis to fair value at death, erasing the decedent's appreciation. The recurring planning insight from TCP Unit 1 recurs here: gift high-basis or rapidly appreciating assets, but hold low-basis appreciated assets until death to capture the step-up. Basis is not a fixed fact — it is a lever set by how property is acquired and transferred.

Like-kind exchanges as deferral

The §1031 like-kind exchange is the premier deferral tool: gain on real property held for business or investment (personal property no longer qualifies post-2017) is deferred when exchanged for like-kind real property, preserved in a carryover basis. The planning value is enormous for a contractor or investor rolling one parcel into another — no tax until an eventual taxable sale, and if the property is held until death, the deferred gain is wiped out by the §1014 step-up. The strict 45-day identification and 180-day completion deadlines, plus the qualified intermediary requirement, are the execution traps a planner manages carefully.

Other deferral and exclusion provisions

Several other provisions defer or exclude gain. §1033 involuntary conversions defer gain when insurance or condemnation proceeds are reinvested in similar property within the replacement period (generally two years; three for condemned business realty). §121 excludes up to $250,000/$500,000 of gain on a principal residence — a planner times a sale around the two-of-five-year ownership/use test. The installment method (§453) spreads gain over the years payments are received, smoothing income across brackets — though it is unavailable for dealer property, losses, and the depreciation-recapture portion (recognized fully in the year of sale). Each is a timing tool the planner deploys to fit the client's bracket and cash needs.

Managing character: capital versus ordinary

The character of gain drives the rate, so steering gain toward capital treatment (0/15/20% versus ordinary rates up to 37%) is core planning. §1231 assets (depreciable business property and land held >1 year) get the best outcome — net gains are capital, net losses are ordinary — subject to the five-year lookback. But depreciation recapture intervenes: §1245 recaptures all prior depreciation on personal property as ordinary income, and §1250 creates unrecaptured §1250 gain on real property taxed at a maximum 25%. A planner anticipates recapture — it can convert an expected capital gain into ordinary income — and structures dispositions accordingly.

Loss planning

Losses are a resource to harvest within limits. Tax-loss harvesting realizes capital losses to offset capital gains (and up to $3,000 of ordinary income, with carryforward), but the wash-sale rule (§1091) disallows the loss if substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after. §267 disallows losses on sales to related parties. For business property, net §1231 losses are fully ordinary (better than capital). The planner harvests losses deliberately — pairing them against gains, respecting the wash-sale and related-party limits, and preferring ordinary loss treatment where the rules allow.

The synthesis — a disposition plan

The planner integrates these tools into a disposition plan: defer gain (§1031, §1033, installment) when the client does not need cash and a lower-rate year is coming; capture the §121 exclusion and the §1014 step-up where possible; manage character around recapture; and harvest losses against gains. The overarching strategy for highly appreciated assets is often "swap till you drop" — exchange under §1031 repeatedly and hold until death, when the step-up erases all the deferred gain. This is the integrative, multi-year property planning that distinguishes TCP from rote rule application.

Holding period, netting, and year-end timing

Beyond basis, the holding period and the netting process shape every disposition. Property held more than one year yields long-term capital gain at preferential rates (0/15/20%); one year or less is short-term at ordinary rates — so a planner near the one-year mark may defer a sale by a few weeks to convert short-term into long-term, a large rate difference for a single decision. Within the year, short-term and long-term gains and losses net separately and then against each other: a net long-term gain keeps its preferential rate, while a net short-term position is taxed as ordinary. The planner sequences sales to optimize this netting — pairing realized losses against the most heavily taxed gains first, and applying the same bracket logic to the capital side by bunching gains into a low-rate year and losses into a high-rate year. Executed across a portfolio of business and investment property, these year-end moves can shift thousands of dollars of tax with no change in the underlying economics.

Mixed-use property and provision interactions

Real-world property is often mixed-use, and the provisions interact in ways that reward careful mapping. A home that was also rented blends the §121 exclusion (on the residence portion) with depreciation recapture — the depreciation taken on the rental use is recaptured as unrecaptured §1250 gain even within the §121 exclusion. Converting a rental into a principal residence before sale can capture part of the exclusion, but it is reduced for periods of non-qualified (rental) use. Property can also flow from a §1031 exchange into a residence, subject to special holding-period rules that prevent abuse. Because the exclusions, recapture, and deferral all turn on the property's use history, the planner reconstructs the purchase, improvement, depreciation, and use records before modeling any sale. The lesson is that a single property can implicate several Code sections at once, and only a full history reveals the tax — property planning is fact-intensive, not formulaic.

CMA bridge

When Jordan Reed sells or exchanges MBG's equipment and land, recapture and §1031 deferral decide the tax. The CFO who plans dispositions — rolling investment land via §1031, timing equipment sales against recapture, and holding the most-appreciated assets for the heirs' step-up — turns the company's property base into a tax-efficient store of value, exactly the planning TCP develops.

Practice and recap

  1. Treat basis as a lever: cost (less depreciation), gift carryover, inherited §1014 step-up; gift high-basis/appreciating, hold low-basis appreciated for the step-up.
  2. Defer with §1031 (real property only; 45/180-day rules), §1033 (reinvest), and §453 installment (spread gain); exclude with §121 ($250k/$500k).
  3. Manage character: §1231 net gain = capital / net loss = ordinary, but §1245 (full) and §1250 (25% unrecaptured) recapture intervene.
  4. Harvest losses against gains within the wash-sale (§1091) and related-party (§267) limits; prefer ordinary §1231 losses.

Recap: property planning controls timing, character, and basis — basis is set by acquisition (cost less depreciation, gift carryover, or inherited §1014 step-up), gains are deferred via §1031 like-kind real-property exchanges, §1033 conversions, and the §453 installment method, and excluded via §121; character is steered toward capital through §1231 while §1245/§1250 recapture is anticipated; losses are harvested against gains within the wash-sale and related-party limits; and the capstone strategy for appreciated assets is to exchange under §1031 and hold until death so the §1014 step-up erases the deferred gain.

flashcards.back: Cost basis (less depreciation), gift = carryover (dual-basis for loss), inherited = §1014 step-up to FMV at death. Gift high-basis/appreciating; hold low-basis appreciated for the step-up.

Defer gain on REAL property (business/investment) exchanged for like-kind real property; carryover basis. 45-day ID / 180-day completion / qualified intermediary. Hold till death → step-up erases deferred gain.

§1033: defer gain on involuntary conversion if reinvested (2 yr / 3 yr realty). §121: exclude $250k/$500k home gain (2-of-5-year test). §453 installment: spread gain over payments (not for dealer/loss/recapture).

§1245: all prior depreciation on personal property recaptured as ordinary. §1250: unrecaptured §1250 gain on realty taxed at max 25%. Anticipate — recapture can turn expected capital gain into ordinary.
Net §1231 gain = long-term capital gain (preferential); net §1231 loss = ordinary (fully deductible). 5-year lookback recharacterizes gain as ordinary up to prior §1231 losses.

Realize capital losses to offset gains (+$3,000 ordinary, carryforward). Wash sale (§1091): loss disallowed if substantially identical bought within 30 days before/after. §267: related-party losses disallowed.
Exchange highly appreciated real property repeatedly under §1031 and hold until death; the §1014 step-up then erases all the deferred gain — a premier wealth strategy.
Capital gains 0/15/20% (LT) vs ordinary up to 37%. Steering gain to capital (via §1231) and avoiding recapture is core property planning.

questions.q: A §1031 like-kind exchange now applies only to:
choices: Real property held for business or investment
questions.explain: Post-2017, §1031 is limited to real property held for business or investment.

questions.q: Holding a highly appreciated asset until death is attractive because:
choices: The §1014 step-up erases the unrealized gain
questions.explain: Inherited property is stepped up to FMV at death, eliminating the decedent's appreciation.

questions.q: Depreciation recapture under §1245 converts gain into:
questions.explain: §1245 recaptures all prior depreciation on personal property as ordinary income.

questions.q: Unrecaptured §1250 gain on real property is taxed at a maximum rate of:
questions.explain: Unrecaptured §1250 gain (prior straight-line depreciation) is taxed at a maximum 25%.

questions.q: The wash-sale rule disallows a loss if substantially identical securities are bought:
choices: Within 30 days before or after the sale
questions.explain: §1091 disallows the loss when substantially identical securities are acquired within 30 days before or after.

questions.q: The installment method may NOT be used for:
choices: The depreciation-recapture portion of a sale
Land sold to an unrelated buyer
questions.explain: Recapture is recognized fully in the year of sale; installment reporting also excludes dealer property and losses.

questions.q: A net §1231 LOSS is treated as:
questions.explain: Net §1231 losses are ordinary; net §1231 gains are capital (the best of both).
